title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys
description: Find the minimum moves to collect all keys in a grid with locks, using BFS over a (row, col, keys bitmask) state space.

sections.title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys

content.title: Shortest Path to Get All Keys

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

A 2D grid contains a starting point @, walls #, empty floor ., lowercase letters (keys) and uppercase letters (locks matching the same letter). Moving 4-directionally, you can walk on floor and keys freely, walk through a lock only if you already hold its matching key, and picking up a key means walking onto its cell. Return the minimum number of moves to collect all keys, or -1 if impossible.

blocks.caption: BFS tracks position together with a bitmask of keys collected so far.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Grid symbols","'@' start, '#' wall, '.' floor, 'a'-'f' keys, 'A'-'F' matching locks"],["Movement","4-directional, one cell per move"],["Lock rule","A lock cell can only be entered if the matching key was already collected"],["Goal","Minimum moves to collect every key present in the grid, or -1"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

This is another grid shortest-path problem, but reachability now depends on which keys have been collected, not just position. Since there are at most 6 possible keys, the set of collected keys can be represented compactly as a bitmask (an integer from 0 to 63), and the BFS state becomes (row, col, keys bitmask).

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Directly extends the Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination pattern: a resource (there, an elimination budget; here, a set of collected keys) becomes part of the BFS state.
3. Understand the Problem

Think of a dungeon explorer collecting keys to unlock doors. A locked door blocks the only path forward until the matching key, perhaps found down a different corridor, is picked up. The explorer wants the fastest route that ends with every key in hand, and the state of "which keys are held" fundamentally changes what paths are open.

blocks.caption: A locked door only opens once the matching key has been collected.

items: At most 6 distinct keys (a through f) exist, so the collected-keys set fits in 6 bits, values 0 to 63.
Walking onto a key cell always adds that key to the current bitmask, even if already held.
Walking onto a lock cell is only legal if the matching key bit is already set in the current bitmask.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
grid = ["@..aA", "..B#.", "....b"]. Start at (0,0), two keys total (a, b), allKeysMask = 0b11 = 3.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: All keys are collected at BFS layer 6, matching the expected output of 6. Note that the lock B at (1,2) is never enterable in this run since key b is only picked up at the very last step, but the path never needed to cross it.
5. How Should We Think?

A plain BFS over (row, col) cannot correctly handle this problem, since the same cell might be legally enterable at one point in the search (with certain keys held) and illegally blocked at another (without them). Worse, a cell might be worth revisiting once new keys open up previously blocked routes through it.

Expanding the state to (row, col, keys bitmask) resolves this cleanly: two visits to the same cell with different key sets are genuinely different situations, and BFS explores this expanded state graph exactly like any other unweighted shortest-path problem, since every move still costs exactly one step.
6. Brute Force Solution
BFS over (row, col, keys) states using a general hash-set for visited, checking for completion (all keys collected) only when a state is dequeued rather than the moment it is generated.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(m * n * 2^k)","k is the number of keys (at most 6); each state is visited once"],["Space","O(m * n * 2^k)","Hash-set visited states plus the BFS queue"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: A hash-set of string keys is correct but slower in practice than a fixed-size 3D boolean array indexed directly by (row, col, keys bitmask), since the bitmask range is small and known in advance (at most 64 values).
8. Optimize the Solution

Replace the hash-set with a 3D boolean array sized exactly m by n by 2^totalKeys, and check for completion the moment a state is generated (not when dequeued), returning immediately at the first BFS layer that reaches the full keys bitmask. Processing the queue strictly layer by layer also makes the step count implicit.

items: Precompute totalKeys and allKeysMask by scanning the grid once.
Use a fixed-size 3D visited array for O(1) lookups instead of hashing string keys.
Check keys == allKeysMask right when a new state is produced, returning the current step count immediately.

10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, hash-set visited","O(m * n * 2^k)","O(m * n * 2^k)"],["Optimized, array-based BFS","O(m * n * 2^k)","O(m * n * 2^k)"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Both approaches share the same asymptotic bound since k is capped at 6; the optimized version is a constant-factor improvement from faster state lookups and earlier termination.
11. Key Takeaways

items: When a small, bounded collection of binary conditions (here, up to 6 keys) affects reachability, encode it as a bitmask and fold it into the BFS state.
A cell can be legitimately revisited if the accompanying non-positional state (keys, budget, color) differs from any prior visit.
Checking the goal condition the moment a new state is generated, rather than when dequeued, avoids one wasted BFS layer.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Shortest Path to Get All Keys extends grid BFS by folding a bitmask of collected keys into the state alongside position, since locks make reachability depend on more than location alone. With at most 6 keys, the state space stays small (m * n * 64 at most), and layer-by-layer BFS finds the minimum number of moves to collect every key, or determines it is impossible.
